info.title: Alchemy
info.description:
Files in, a graph out: entities, relations, chunks and vectors, each
carrying where it came from and how it was produced.

This document is generated from alchemy.proto and describes a
gateway in front of a gRPC service. The gRPC service is the product;
this is a translation of it, offered because a buyer evaluating
Alchemy should be able to curl it and because browsers exist
(DESIGN.md §6). Anything the two disagree about is a bug in the
gateway, never a feature of it.

**Review has no route here, and that is deliberate.** `Review` is a
bidirectional stream: a reviewer answers item three while item four
is still arriving, and a decision reaches an extraction that has not
run yet. HTTP/1.1 has no shape for that — a request body must be
finished before its response can be read — so translating it would
produce polling plus a submit endpoint, which is the thing §6
rejected gRPC-over-HTTP for in the first place. Rather than ship a
route that deadlocks, `POST /v1/jobs/{job_id}/review` answers **501
Not Implemented** with a sentence naming the gRPC method. Use
`alchemy.v1.Alchemy/Review` over gRPC. A job held at
`JOB_STATE_NEEDS_REVIEW` (§7.3) can be watched, fetched and deleted
over HTTP; it can only be *unblocked* over gRPC.

**The two streaming routes** — `GET /v1/jobs/{id}/events` and
`GET /v1/jobs/{id}/result:stream` — answer with a stream of JSON
objects, one per line (`application/json`), each wrapping the
message in `{"result": …}` or, if the stream fails partway,
`{"error": …}`. Send `Accept: text/event-stream` and the same
objects arrive as Server-Sent Events instead, for the benefit of
`EventSource`. The events, and their order, are identical.

**Uploading a corpus.** `POST /v1/sources` accepts either a stream
of JSON `SourceChunk` objects or — the way a human uploads a 10GB
dump — the raw bytes with `Content-Type: application/octet-stream`
and the metadata in the query string:
`?name=dump.sql&kind=SOURCE_KIND_DDL&media_type=application/sql`.
Either way the bytes are forwarded a frame at a time and spooled to
disk; nothing buffers the file (§8.4).

**Error codes.** The gRPC codes arrive as: `NOT_FOUND` 404,
`INVALID_ARGUMENT` 400, `FAILED_PRECONDITION` **412**,
`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED` **429**, `UNAUTHENTICATED` 401, `CANCELLED`
499, `INTERNAL` 500. 412 rather than 400 for `FAILED_PRECONDITION`
is the one deliberate departure from the gateway's defaults: the
service separates "this request can never be valid" from "this
request is fine and the job is not ready yet", and collapsing both
to 400 would tell half of all callers to stop retrying something
that will work in a minute. 429 is §8.4's "try later" and is the one
refusal a retry loop should act on.

post.summary: Assert records a fact somebody knows and no document states.
post.description:
It is not a hole in §4. Nothing is stored that a job does not already
store, the graph comes back as JSON, and where it goes afterwards is the
caller's business exactly as it is for every other result. What it removes
is a detour: until now the only way in was to write the fact into a file,
upload it, create a job, poll it and fetch the result — five steps and an
invented document for one triple — and it arrived stamped
PRODUCER_GRAPH_IMPORT, "an existing graph already asserted it", which is
not what happened and cost the record the one thing that made it worth
admitting: a person who can be asked.

It is synchronous, and that is not an optimisation. An assertion has no
chunking, no model call and no embedding; it is a parse and a check
against the ontology. There is nothing to poll, and returning a job id for
a caller to poll would be inventing asynchrony an operation does not have.
The Result carries the job id in its `job` field, so the record is still
traceable through GetJob like any other.

The ontology is optional and checked when given, which is the rule graph
sources already follow. An assertion under an ontology that does not
declare its types comes back with violations naming them, rather than a
refusal: §5 makes the graph never more permissive than the vocabulary, and
a person asserting a type nobody declared is exactly the case that has to
be visible instead of quietly accepted.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description:
AssertRequest is a fact a person states.

The entities and relations are given in the same shape every other producer
emits, and their provenance is overwritten rather than read: the producer is
PRODUCER_HUMAN, the source is the asserter, and by/at are stamped by the
server from `by` and its own clock. A caller cannot assert something on
somebody else's behalf by filling the field in, and cannot backdate one.

post.summary: Unary for things that are one question.

400.description:
The request could not be valid for any state of the world — no
sources, a source nobody uploaded, or a document source with no
ontology (§5 has no unconstrained extraction mode). Retrying it
unchanged will fail identically.

401.description: No bearer token, or one the service does not accept.

429.description:
§8.4's admission control. The service declares its capacity and
refuses beyond it rather than accepting work it cannot hold. This
is the refusal to retry on; a rejected job is an operator's
problem for a minute, an accepted job that dies is their problem
for an afternoon.

get.summary:
Progress is server-streaming: stages, counts, and conflicts as they are
found rather than at the end.
get.description:
Over HTTP this is newline-delimited JSON, and Server-Sent Events when the
caller asks for them by Accept. Same events, same order. §6 called SSE "a
stream pretending to be a response" and that is still true; it is offered
because EventSource is all a browser has, and §6's own reason for a
gateway is that browsers exist.

401.description: No bearer token, or one the service does not accept.

get.summary:
ListFindings and Decide are review for a job that has already stopped, and
they are the reason the paragraph above is about mid-run review rather
than about review.
get.description:
What Review's bidirectional shape buys is that a decision reaches an
extraction that has not run yet. That property is real and it is
untranslatable: a reviewer answers item three while item four is still
arriving, and an HTTP request body must be finished before its response is
read. So Review stays unannotated and the gateway still answers its path
501.

A job sitting at NEEDS_REVIEW is not that situation. Nothing is running.
There is no item four. The findings are a finite list in a finished result
and the decisions are a batch, so a list and a batch is not a degradation
of the stream — it is what that case actually is, and forcing it through a
bidirectional connection was making every HTTP client pay for a property
this case does not have. The consequence until now was that a buyer could
curl the graph and could not curl "this edge is wrong".

The two shapes are one mechanism: a decision submitted here is the same
ReviewDecision, applied by the same code, and lands in the same
provenance. What differs is when it may be sent.

No bearer token, or one the service does not accept.

404.description: No such job, or one the retention sweep already dropped.

412.description:
The job has no result to give yet. Either it is still running, or
it is held at NEEDS_REVIEW because two sources disagree and §7.3
will not let a caller opt out of a person — or the result is too
large for one message and the body names
`/v1/jobs/{job_id}/result:stream` instead.

parameters.name: page_size
parameters.description:
Records per page, honoured only by StreamResult. Zero means the server's
default, which is picked so a page stays well under the 4MB limit.

get.summary:
A large result is not one message; see §8.4. gRPC's default limit is 4MB
and a large import blows through it, so GetResult refuses a result that
does not fit rather than truncating one, and points here.
get.description:
Over HTTP the refusal is kept even though HTTP has no such limit: a
gateway that quietly served what gRPC refused would be the second source
of truth. A custom verb rather than a query parameter because a flag that
changes the shape of a response is two routes pretending to be one.

post.summary: Upload is client-streaming: a corpus is not a field in a message.
post.description:
body:"*" is the only mapping a client stream allows, and it makes the
request body a sequence of SourceChunk messages rather than one — which is
what keeps §8.4 true over HTTP too: a frame is decoded and forwarded at a
time, so a 10GB dump is never a 10GB buffer. The path takes no parameters
because a client-streaming method cannot bind them; the first frame names
the source, exactly as it does over gRPC.

401.description: No bearer token, or one the service does not accept.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description:
SourceChunk is one frame of an upload. The metadata fields are read from the
first frame only and ignored afterwards, so a client streaming a 10GB dump
repeats no headers and the server holds no per-frame state beyond the file
handle it is writing to. (streaming inputs)

AlchemyDecideBody.description:
DecideRequest is a batch of decisions about one job.

A batch and not one decision, because the queue a person works through is a
list and answering it one HTTP request at a time would make the round trips
the cost of reviewing rather than the thinking. Order is preserved: two
decisions about one item apply in the order given, which is what makes
"reject, then always" mean what it reads as.

protobufNullValue.description:
`NullValue` is a singleton enumeration to represent the null value for the
`Value` type union.

 The JSON representation for `NullValue` is JSON `null`.

 - NULL_VALUE: Null value.

by.description:
Who is asserting. Required — see the by field on Provenance, and
preflight's assertion_unsigned.

note.description:
Why, in the asserter's own words. It lands on every record's attributes
under "note", because a fact stated with a reason is a different thing to
audit from one stated without.

supersedes.description:
What this assertion replaces. Each entry names a record — an Entity.id or
a Relation identity — and says why.

A person who knows the CTO changed is stating two things: that Bruno holds
the office, and that Ada no longer does. Without this only the first had
a shape, and the second arrived as a new edge beside the old one while the
graph reported itself clean. The claim is carried, never executed; see
Supersession.

v1AssertRequest.description:
AssertRequest is a fact a person states.

The entities and relations are given in the same shape every other producer
emits, and their provenance is overwritten rather than read: the producer is
PRODUCER_HUMAN, the source is the asserter, and by/at are stamped by the
server from `by` and its own clock. A caller cannot assert something on
somebody else's behalf by filling the field in, and cannot backdate one.

strategy.description:
One of fixed, sentence, paragraph, heading, semantic, whole. Empty means
the default of §7.1 — heading falling back to paragraph then fixed.

overlap.description:
Overlap is the cheap insurance against the split-relation problem, and is
non-zero by default. A negative value is refused rather than clamped.

v1Chunking.description:
Chunking is a job input for the same reason models are: the person who knows
the corpus is the caller (§7.1).

v1Conflict.description:
Conflict is two sources both claiming to be right, with nothing in the data
to decide between them. It is returned whether or not review is on, so a
caller running unattended still learns that its sources disagree rather than
receiving whichever edge happened to be written last.

v1ConflictKind.description:
- CONFLICT_KIND_CARDINALITY: Two records assert an edge of a type the ontology declared at_most_one_in
or at_most_one_out, at the end it constrained. The only conflict kind that
compares two claims about one NODE rather than about one edge, and the one
that makes a fact able to go out of date.

chunks_empty.description:
Chunks that produced nothing. A high number means extraction is failing
quietly.

chunks_unread.description:
Source text that could not be read at all — a scanned page with no OCR
model supplied. §5: never silently returned as empty.

dropped.description:
Records a standing rule (§5c's `always`) removed without anybody being
asked about them. Everything else a graph is missing is reported
somewhere; a record a written policy dropped before any queue was shown
would otherwise leave the result one record shorter and say nothing.

duplicates.description:
Pairs of nodes that may be one node. It is in this block because it is a
number no reader can derive from the entities beside it — both nodes are
well-formed, correctly typed and separately attributable — and because
"one node in six may be a duplicate" is exactly a number needed to
distrust a graph. It counts the findings, not the pairs still unjoined, so
it does not fall when a merge is applied: which of them were answered is
in each finding's provenance.

chunks.description:
How many chunks and vectors the job produced.

They are here because §8.4 pages a large result and this block rides on
the first page: a consumer streaming a graph knew how many entities it had
seen of how many and could say nothing of the sort about chunks or
vectors. They are also the denominator that makes chunks_empty and
chunks_unread readable — "23 chunks produced nothing" is a different
corpus at 30 chunks than at 3000.

v1Counts.description:
Counts is what makes the difference between a graph you can act on and one
you merely have (§5).

source_ids.description:
Source IDs handed back by UploadSource. Naming an unknown one is refused
rather than skipped: a job that quietly imports three of the four files it
was given produces a graph whose gaps nobody can explain.

ontology.description:
Required for document sources (§5). There is no unconstrained mode: the
74%→94% story is the argument, and shipping the ungoverned version would
mean shipping the 74%.

idempotency_key.description:
Supplying an idempotency key makes creation idempotent. A client whose
call timed out cannot know whether the job was admitted, and both blind
answers are expensive: retry and a 10GB dump is imported twice, give up
and the night's work is silently lost.

part.description:
Which part of the ontology this corpus is read under and checked against.
The ontology is partitioned by provenance (§2.1's third lesson): telling a
prose extractor it may emit `function` and `calls` invites it to invent
code structure out of documentation, so a job names one part and gets one
vocabulary.

Empty means "prose". That is a decision, not a placeholder: §5's first
release is documents and entity extraction, a document is prose, and every
request written before this field existed meant a prose job. A required
field would have invalidated all of them, and proto3 gives no way to tell
an unset string from an empty one — so the default has to be the meaning
those callers already had rather than a refusal they never asked for.

rejected.description:
Decisions the job did not recognise, by item id, with the reason. An
unknown item is reported rather than refused: a batch assembled from a
list somebody read ten minutes ago may name an item a rule has since
taken away, and failing the whole batch over it would lose the decisions
that were still good.

v1DecideResponse.description:
DecideResponse says what the batch did and what is left.

remaining_holding is the number that matters: it is zero when the job can
finish, and a caller that submitted decisions and got a non-zero back knows
it is not done without having to re-list.

left.description:
Left is the node whose name is contained in the other's, which is a
property of the pair rather than of the order they were extracted in.
Neither side is the wrong one.

v1Duplicate.description:
Duplicate is two nodes that may be one node, and are not joined.

It is a third kind of finding beside Violation and Conflict because it is
neither. A violation is one source saying something the ontology does not
allow — a declared rule was broken, and the graph minus the record is still
usable. Neither is true here: no vocabulary forbids two names for one thing,
and removing either node takes its edges with it. A conflict is two sources
both claiming to be right with nothing to decide between them, and these two
records do not disagree; they agree and are merely not joined. So nothing is
wrong, the graph is delivered, and what is owed is the pair and the number.

v1DuplicateSide.description:
DuplicateSide is one node of a candidate pair, with what a reviewer needs to
answer without a lookup: which node, what it is called, and where it came
from.

v1DuplicateSignal.description:
DuplicateSignal names the deterministic evidence that two nodes may be one
thing. It is on the finding because a reviewer answering "are these the
same?" is entitled to know what asked them.

 - DUPLICATE_SIGNAL_NAME_AFFIX: Under one type, one node's name is the other's with whole words added at
the front or the back: "document" and "document package". It is the shape
a per-chunk extractor produces, since each chunk is a separate call that
cannot see how the others named the thing.
 - DUPLICATE_SIGNAL_NAME_ACROSS_PRODUCERS: Under one type, two nodes with different ids fold to the same name and two
different producers made them. Ids this pipeline mints are a function of
type and name, so equal names are already one node; ids a source supplies
— a graph import's, an assertion's — are not, and that is the only case
this fires on.

type.description:
An empty field is one the reviewer did not touch. A reviewer who retyped
an entity said nothing about its name, and a message that carried both
would silently blank the half they left alone.

into.description:
The entity id this record is the same record as: the answer to a duplicate
item, and the only correction that changes which node a record is rather
than what it says. It is a field on Edit rather than a fifth verb because
§5c's four are a closed set, and a merge is an edit that corrects which
node a record belongs to, exactly as from and to correct which nodes an
edge runs between. It could not be spelled with `name`: an id is derived
once, by the producer that made the record, so renaming the absorbed node
to the survivor's spelling leaves two nodes with one name and every edge
where it was.

holding.description:
How many of the items below are conflicts nobody has answered — the ones
holding the job under §7.3. The rest are findings a reader may act on and
the job does not wait for.

v1Findings.description:
Findings is that queue, as a list rather than as a stream.

The job's state travels with it because the list alone cannot say why it is
empty: a SUCCEEDED job with nothing to review and a job still RUNNING both
have no findings yet, and a client that could not tell would report "all
clear" for a job that has not finished looking.

v1Guess.description:
Guess is an inferred mapping the pipeline made and is obliged to report.
§2.1: a guess that does not announce itself is a bug with a three-month fuse.

expires_at.description:
When un-reviewed work is discarded. §5c: without it the "stateless"
service quietly grows a database of abandoned reviews.

counts.description: Counts so far, not at the end.

conflict.description:
§7.3: a conflict is emitted when it is found. An operator watching a
two-hour import should learn in minute three that it will need them, not
at minute one hundred and twenty.

model_calls.description:
§7.2: a running total, so a job whose bill is growing faster than expected
can be cancelled while it runs rather than after it finishes.

model_calls_by_stage.description:
The same total broken down, for the operator who wants to know which stage
is spending it.

v1JobState.description:
JobState is where a job is. NEEDS_REVIEW is reachable without review mode
being on, because a conflict always requires a person (§7.3).

v1ModelCall.description:
ModelCall records what a job spent. §7.2: cost is not optimised for, but it
is never hidden.

api_key.description:
Deliberately per call rather than a server-side secret: the service never
holds a buyer's credentials between jobs, which is the same reasoning as
§4 applied to keys instead of graphs.

v1ModelEndpoint.description:
ModelEndpoint is one of the caller's models. The name is not decoration: it
is what appears in provenance and in the cost report, so two runs against
two models are told apart by a reader who has only the result.

ocr.description:
Absent OCR is a supported configuration, not an error: §5 says a scanned
page is then reported as unread, never silently returned as empty text.

v1Producer.description:
Producer is §5b's "field that matters": DDL and GRAPH_IMPORT mean a machine
read something that already said this, LLM_EXTRACT means a model decided it.

 - PRODUCER_HUMAN: A named person asserted it. The only producer whose source is not a
document, and the only one for which by/at below are required.

records.description: How many records used it: what tells a vocabulary gap from a typo.

from.description:
The entity types this relation type was observed between, sorted. Empty
for an entity proposal, and for a relation whose ends are themselves
undeclared — a line proposing two undeclared things at once is a line
nobody can accept as one thing.

sources.description:
Who used it. §5b's question asked of a proposal: a type every record of
one PDF used is a different suggestion from one a person asserted by name.

example.description: One record that used it, so a reader can go and look.

v1Proposal.description:
Proposal is a type a source used that the ontology does not declare, stated
as the change that would let it.

Not a second violation. A violation is per record and says what is wrong;
six records using one undeclared type are six violations, and a
four-hundred-thousand-record import missing one type is four hundred
thousand of them. This is one entry per type and it says what to do.

It proposes and never applies. The ends and the counts are observed —
"MEMBER_OF was used four times, always from Person to Team, by liliang" —
and whether that is what the type MEANS is a judgement §2.1 will not let a
machine make.

Produced only when a vocabulary was supplied. A run with no ontology has
nothing to be undeclared against, and the way to ask "what vocabulary would
this graph need" is to supply an empty one — a question rather than a side
effect of not asking.

v1ProposalKind.description: ProposalKind says which of an ontology's two lists a proposal belongs in.

chunk.description: -1 when the producer did not work in chunks (DDL, graph import).

chunking.description:
The chunking strategy that produced the chunk. §7.1: a graph re-extracted
under a different strategy is a different graph.

reviewed_by.description:
§5c: review adds to provenance, it does not overwrite it — a reviewed edge
still says a model proposed it.

rule_set.description:
Names the standing `always` policy (§5c) already in force when this
record was extracted: the name of the set, resolved through
Result.rule_sets, not the set itself. Distinct from reviewed_by: a rule is
applied to everything it covers at the end of the job, so reviewed_by
lands on the chunk that ran before the rule existed too. This says the
model that proposed *this* record had already been told.

It carries a name because the shapes are identical on every record and
this field is on every record: a fifty-rule policy spelled out is four
kilobytes, §8's import is four hundred thousand records, and the correct
answer weighed more than the graph. The name is fixed-width, so a run
under fifty rules costs a record exactly what a run under one does.

Field 9 held those spelled-out shapes. It keeps the number and changes
its name because the meaning changed: a client still reading `rules` gets
a decoding failure it can see rather than a digest it would go on
splitting on "; ". Nothing persists a result (§4), so the only readers
are live ones, and a loud break is the one to give them.

ruled_by.description:
The one rule that actually acted on this record — retyped it, renamed it,
or answered the question it raised — by the name rule_sets uses.

rule_set says which rules were in the room; this says which one moved.
Empty means none did, which is not the same as none being in force.

by.description:
Who asserted this, for PRODUCER_HUMAN. Required for that producer and
meaningless for the others, whose sources are documents.

Not reviewed_by. That says somebody accepted a record another producer
proposed, and the record still names the proposer; this says nobody
proposed it and a person is the whole of its authority. A reader filtering
to "what a machine read" excludes these and keeps the reviewed ones.

at.description: When the assertion was made, RFC 3339.

v1Provenance.description:
Provenance says where a fact came from and how it was produced. Every entity
and every relation carries one; §5b makes this a product guarantee rather
than a debugging aid.

key.description:
Which of several parallel edges this is; see Relation.key. Without it a
decision about one end of a connection acts on both.

provenance.description:
Narrows the Ref to the records one source produced. A conflict names two
claims about one subject and a decision is about one of them, so without
this a rejection would delete the side the reviewer kept.

Set on a review target and unset on a Violation.about, and the asymmetry is
the difference between the two questions. A decision acts on the records
one source produced, so the source is part of what it names; a violation
already carries its own provenance beside the ref, and repeating it inside
would be two answers to one question that can disagree.

v1Ref.description:
Ref names graph records by what they say rather than by index: an index into
a slice stops meaning anything the moment a rejection removes an element.

key.description:
The producer's own name for this edge, and what makes two parallel edges
two edges: a table that references another twice — once per end of a
connection between two of its rows — states two foreign keys, and from,
to and type cannot tell them apart. Empty when the producer has no name
for its edges, which is every model-extracted graph. See
alchemy.Relation.Key for the whole argument.

job.description:
The job that produced this graph, and the only identity a result has.

It was missing, and every store written against this message had to invent
something: two demanded a run id from their caller, and two independently
digested the whole encoded result — an identity that changes whenever this
message grows a field, so every previously loaded corpus is orphaned by an
upgrade nobody consulted the store about. The service had the answer all
along and simply never put it here.

Empty is a graph nobody named, and it means what it says: a store must not
pretend it can recognise this result again.

rules.description:
The `always` rules this job's review produced. They are returned rather
than kept because §4 means the service holds no policy between jobs: the
caller keeps them and supplies them on the next job, which is how a
pipeline that started attended becomes one that runs itself without ever
having guessed (§7.3).

duplicates.description:
Two nodes that may be one node, returned whether or not review is on for
the same reason violations are: a caller running unattended is owed the
numbers needed to distrust what it got.

rule_sets.description:
Every standing policy this job's records were extracted under, each named
once. Provenance.rule_set is a name into this list.

A second field rather than a widening of `rules`, and the difference is
the whole point. `rules` is this job's output: what its review decided,
for the caller to keep and hand to the next job. This is its input:
whatever the model had already been told, including an authored rule that
was in force and matched nothing — which will never appear in `rules` and
is exactly the rule a reader chasing a name from a record needs to
resolve. Widening `rules` to cover both would leave a caller round-tripping
it as their policy while re-declaring somebody else's rules as their own
job's finding, and would leave every existing reader holding a field whose
meaning had quietly changed underneath them.

supersessions.description: What this run says is no longer true, and who said so.

proposals.description:
The types this corpus used and the ontology does not declare, one per type
rather than one per record.

page.description: Zero-based, so a client can tell a resumed stream from a fresh one.

job.description:
The job that produced this graph, on the first page with the rest of the
summary. A client already knows what it asked for; what it does not have
is a way to hand the reassembled pages on as a complete Result, and a
consumer that had to remember the request in order to fill in the identity
is one that will fill in the wrong one after a retry.

counts.description: Set on the first page only.

rule_sets.description:
The policies the records on every page were extracted under. They ride on
the first page with the rest of the summary, and for the same reason: a
reader deciding whether to trust a paged graph is deciding on what the
model was told, and making them pay for every entity first would be making
the answer arrive after the decision.

v1ResultPage.description:
ResultPage is one page of a large result (§8.4). The summary rides on the
first page rather than the last: an operator who wants the numbers needed to
distrust the graph should get them before deciding whether to read it, not
after paying for every entity.

job_id.description:
The first message on the stream must name the job; later ones may repeat
it or leave it empty. A first message with a job_id and no item_id is how
a reviewer attaches to a queue without deciding anything yet.

by.description:
Who decided. Required: a decision nobody signed cannot be written into
provenance, and "reviewed by" with nobody in it is worse than not claiming
review at all.

index.description: Where the finding sits in the matching Result slice.

shape.description:
The class of mistake this item belongs to, and what an `always` rule is
matched on.

suppressed_by.description:
The rule that already answered this item's class. An item carrying one is
not a question — it is an answer already given, sent rather than dropped
so that a queue three items shorter than the findings can say which rule
took each away.

v1ReviewKind.description:
ReviewKind is §5c's ranking table as a set.

The numbers are wire identity and cannot be reordered, so DUPLICATE is 5
while it ranks fourth — below a guess, because nothing about a duplicate is
wrong and an unanswered one leaves the graph exactly as the extractor
produced it, and above low confidence, because the answer decides what every
edge on both nodes points at. The rank a client should sort by is on the
item; this enum says which question it is, not which is more urgent.

enabled.description:
Review is a mode, not a stage everything passes through (§5c). Leaving
this false still gets conflicts queued, because a conflict holds the job
either way and the queue is how it gets unblocked.

min_confidence.description:
The line below which an inferred record is queued as low confidence. Zero
queues none: a caller who has not said what "unsure" means for their model
has not asked a question.

rules.description:
Rules already recorded by an earlier `always`. Carried per job because the
service stores nothing between jobs (§4) — the caller keeps its own policy.

from.description:
For an authored rule this is the declaration itself — the same verb,
person, note and moment, asserted in advance rather than in answer to an
item, and carrying no item_id because no item was answered. An authored
rule is refused unless it names a person, states a reason in `because` and
says when it was declared; and it may not be about a conflict, because
§7.3's escape hatch is a rule made by somebody who had seen one.

v1ReviewRule.description:
ReviewRule is a class of question that has already been answered: either by
an `always` on an item, or by a person who wrote the rule down before any
job ran. Either way it carries what produced it: a rule without an origin is
an unexplainable policy (§5c).

v1ReviewVerb.description:
ReviewVerb is what a reviewer did. §5c lists exactly four and the set is
closed: a fifth would be a way of disposing of a proposal that the
provenance of the result has no way to describe.

 - REVIEW_VERB_ALWAYS: ALWAYS accepts this one and stops the queue asking about ones like it.

v1RuleOrigin.description:
RuleOrigin is which warrant a rule has. They are different claims about the
same suppression: REVIEWED says a person looked at this exact finding and
generalised from it, AUTHORED says a person declared it in advance having
seen no instance. A reader who cannot tell them apart reads the weaker one
as the stronger.

 - RULE_ORIGIN_UNSPECIFIED: UNSPECIFIED is read as REVIEWED, and that is a decision rather than a
placeholder: every rule that could exist before this field did was minted
from a decision on an item, so the wire default has to mean what the
callers who wrote it meant. An authored rule has to say so, which is the
direction that fails safe — a lost marker under-claims.

name.description:
A digest over exactly the members below, computed the way a cache address
is (§8.2): length-prefixed framing, SHA-256, byte-exact across processes
and architectures, so that two nodes running halves of one job (§8.3) name
one policy one way. A reader can recompute it from the members and check.

v1RuleSet.description:
RuleSet is the standing policy in force at one moment of a job, named so a
record can point at it rather than repeat it.

There is more than one per job because the set changes while the job runs:
§6 chose a stream so that "a person working a queue wants their decisions to
take effect on work still running", so a rule made in minute three is in
force for minute four and was not in force for minute two.

v1Source.description:
Source is the handle a CreateJob names. It is not the bytes: those are on
disk, and every reader works from a stream.

v1SourceChunk.description:
SourceChunk is one frame of an upload. The metadata fields are read from the
first frame only and ignored afterwards, so a client streaming a 10GB dump
repeats no headers and the server holds no per-frame state beyond the file
handle it is writing to.

v1SourceKind.description: SourceKind is which of the four readers handles a source (§2).

name.description:
The rule's identity: its origin and its shape, as
"authored:violation/unknown_entity_type/type=Flag/producer=llm-extract".
The origin is in the name because "a person decided this finding" and "a
person declared this in advance" are different warrants for the same
suppression, and a name that rendered them identically would let the
weaker be read as the stronger.

told.description:
The sentence the model was shown: the stated reason, what to do about it,
and who said so. A shape says which class was suppressed; only this says
what the model was asked to stop doing and on whose word.

v1StandingRule.description:
StandingRule is one rule of a set: what it is called, and what the model was
told about it.

provenance.description:
Who is making this claim — the supersession's own provenance, not the
superseding record's. A reviewer may retire a record a model proposed, and
those are two claims by two parties.

v1Supersession.description:
Supersession is one record saying another is over.

retires is an Entity.id or a Relation identity, and it deliberately need not
be present in this result: the thing being replaced is usually in a store
from a run that finished last month.

Alchemy never acts on one. §4 means it holds no graph and could not, and a
producer that could delete another producer's fact by naming it would be
§2.1 with write access. Where both records are in one result the
disagreement is CONFLICT_KIND_CARDINALITY and §7.3 still stops the job. What
this carries is that the statement survives the pipeline: a store can act on
it deliberately, and a reader months later can see that somebody said the
old answer was over, and name them.

v1Unread.description:
Unread exists so that "no text here" is never indistinguishable from "an
empty page".

subject.description:
The subject rendered for a person: an entity id, or "from -[type]-> to".
It is what a review item is filed under and what a standing rule matches
on, so it is unchanged; `about` is the same subject in fields.

about.description:
The record this violation is about, in fields rather than in prose.

§5b promises a wrong record is "checkable, correctable, and excludable",
and excludable was the word that failed: a consumer holding the graph and
the findings could only join them by parsing "a -[USES]-> b" back into
three fields, which is a private copy of the verifier's output format that
no test on either side would notice drifting. Duplicate got this right
from the start with left.id and right.id.

Unset for a violation about something that is not a graph record — a
malformed row and an unnamed column are about a file, and a ref for them
would be a join that resolves to nothing.

v1ViolationKind.description:
- VIOLATION_KIND_MALFORMED_ROW: The kinds above are ontology-shaped. The four below are source-shaped — a
file that does not fit its own header, which is a way a table can fail and
a schema cannot.

BearerToken.description:
`Authorization: Bearer <token>`. The header is forwarded
verbatim to the gRPC service as `authorization` metadata, which
is the only thing that decides whether it is valid — the gateway
holds no credential of its own and has no opinion about yours.
A request with no bearer header at all is refused by the gateway
with 401 before it reaches the service, so that every route
including the 501 above answers the same way to an anonymous
caller.
BearerToken.name: Authorization
